turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr Pemberton, do come in. The computer is still thinking about it, so I may be a bit stop-start.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I took the early bus so that I would not keep you waiting.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Very sensible. Right, I think this is your record. What brings you in today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It is my diabetes review. The home readings have been rather higher than I would like, and I felt I ought to come and say so.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, could you say that again? I had clicked into someone else's cardiology letter.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly. My finger-prick sugars have been up. I have had type two diabetes for twelve years, which I believe is already on your screen.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Twelve years, yes, still on the problem list. Arrival blood pressure was one thirty-two over seventy-eight, and the pulse was seventy-six. What are you actually taking?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin, one gram twice a day, with breakfast and with my evening meal. I do not miss those.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And there is insulin on here as well.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. Lantus, that is insulin glargine. I inject fourteen units at bedtime.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fourteen? The nurse who went through your medicines this morning has typed eighteen units. Would you say the dose once more?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Fourteen units. Dr Shah reduced me to fourteen last autumn, and I have stayed there. I think the nurse misheard.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): So that is fourteen from you and eighteen on her entry, and the old prescription will not load. I am going to leave the figure unsettled. Do you inject it every night?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I do try, Doctor. On the days I am at the council archives I sometimes do not get round to it. I finish late, and I am very tired by then.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days is the archives?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days a week, Monday, Wednesday and Friday. I miss the bedtime injection on most of those evenings, so perhaps two or three times a week. I am sorry. I know that is not what was intended.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): The metformin, though, you take as prescribed?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Both doses, every day, without fail.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me the numbers on the meter, if you can.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The fasting one was one-eighty-something, I think, though that might actually have been the bedtime reading. I had one-sixty in the notebook, and a two-hundred-and-something after Sunday lunch. I do get them muddled. They are higher than my usual, which sat in the low hundreds.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): One-eighty-something, fasting or otherwise. I am not putting a guess in the record. Could you give me the fasting figure again, slowly?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I honestly cannot separate them, Doctor. One hundred and eighty-something is the number that stays in my mind, but I may have the time of day wrong.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the meter out of it, then. Any tingling or numbness in the feet?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): A little tingling in the toes, mostly at night, for a few months. Not pain, exactly.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any sores, cracks, or signs of infection on the feet?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort. I do look when I take my socks off.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the eyes. Has the vision changed at all since your last screening?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): The photographs were last spring, I believe. As for the vision, mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really. If I am tired the print goes a shade soft, but I would not call it a proper problem.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I shall not count that as a yes. Shoes and socks off, please, and I will look at the feet.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly, Doctor.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Skin is intact, no ulcer on either foot, and the pulses are there. Monofilament feeling is a bit dull over the right toes. The left side is normal.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I had rather thought the right side felt woollier.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath on walking?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. Neither of those.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels, and the waterworks, anything new apart from the diabetes itself?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I am passing urine more at night, perhaps twice, which I have put down to the sugars. The bowels are quite regular.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): And thirst?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, noticeably more thirsty these past three weeks or so.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired with it?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): A little weary in the afternoons, yes.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): If I may add one thing, my sister Margaret posted me a bottle of biotin, the capsules she takes for her own nails. I have not opened them. I should not like to start her medicine without your say-so.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please don't take your sister's biotin. It is not for you, and it will do nothing for the diabetes. Looking at the missed jabs, I was going to increase the Lantus to twenty units from tonight.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): If you feel that is the right course, Doctor, I will of course follow it.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Actually, no, scratch that. My impression, and it is only provisional, is that the high readings are coming from the missed injections rather than the dose being too small. I will not put the insulin up, and I will not change the metformin either.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I quite understand. Thank you for explaining it.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will ask the diabetes specialist nurse to see you about getting the evening injection done on archive days, and I will send bloods today for an HbA1c and kidney function.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): That is very kind. Ought I to come back to you?

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. I will see you here in six weeks with the results. Between now and then, please inject every night, archive days included, and write each sugar down with the time of day so we are not guessing.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall. Quite off the medical subject, if you will indulge me, my grandson was Bottom in the school Midsummer Night's Dream on Saturday. He was terribly proud.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was he indeed. Hang on, the screen has just refreshed and eaten my last line. Do go on, I can listen while it reloads.

[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): The traffic back from the hall was perfectly dreadful, and then the rain came down in sheets. We sat in the car for a good forty minutes by the roundabout. He still had a little of the donkey head under his arm, which did make the other drivers stare.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha. Nothing in that for the notes. Sorry, I half thought you had said a cough in among the traffic. Was there a cough, or a fever? No, ignore me, that was the weather.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough and no fever, Doctor. Only the rain, and a rather long queue. I am quite well in that respect.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Reception will book the six-week visit, and the nurse will telephone you about her slot. Mind how you go in that rain.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
